R286.summary: Ciphered despatches of Giovanni Battista Pallotto, nuncio to the Emperor, to Cardinal Francesco Barberini, Vienna, August-November 1629, on the Mantuan succession crisis: Pallotto's attempts, through P. Valeriano Magno and the imperial minister Eggenberg, to mediate between the Emperor and the French envoy Sabran over Casale, Susa and the Grisons passes. Kiewning (Nuntiaturberichte IV/2, 1897) prints the contemporary decipherments from the Rome-received copies. R286 (4 Aug 1629) is Kiewning Nr. 153, opening 'ho riceuto la risposta datami in scritto'.
R286.en:
I have received the answer given me in writing to the request I made by the note, a copy of which I sent with the last
post. Not only do they persist in their first views, but they show that they have entirely forgotten what His Majesty,
Prince Eggenberg and other leading ministers heard from me again and again at the very time when His Majesty's letter
was delivered to Our Lord: the reasons concerning the public peace, but more precisely the interests of the crown of
Spain and of the House of Austria, for which His Beatitude judged it well not to make the representations asked for in
that letter; and finally the effort His Beatitude chose to make to hold back the coming of the King of France into Italy
by sending an extraordinary nuncio, and the reason that delayed it, which was the representations and declarations of
the Count of Monterrey.

R287.summary: End of the 4 August despatch: Sabran's courier to the King, Spanish suspicion that the French aim at the Empire, the reasons the Emperor's ministers give for war in Italy.
R287.en:
‹Nevertheless, after a long discussion, it was drawn from what he said that he would sound out the King's mind in the
manner indicated, provided that the civil and unarmed possession of the states were declared to mean that the Emperor
would acquire it› through a commissioner of his who was not distrusted by the Duke of Mantua, and that no change or
alteration whatever would be made in the civil, political and military government of the two states, nor in the
treatment, pre-eminences and prerogatives of the person and family of the Duke. Provided that justice were declared to
be done by the ordinary way and in conformity with the imperial laws and constitutions, and that the succession to the
said states were judged according to the rights that belonged to each of the parties at the time of the death of the
last Duke Vincenzo.

R288.summary: The new Bohemian bishoprics and the Emperor's complaints about P. Valeriano Magni's writings on the Carolina and his alchemy and mines; Pallotto asks for orders.
R288.en:
On the matter of the new bishoprics to be erected in Bohemia, I see what Your Most Illustrious Lordship commands me, and
in accordance with it I shall seek to bring it about in due time, not without hope of achieving it.

I informed His Majesty that the brief and other papers had arrived for carrying out the business of the church property
in Bohemia, taking the occasion to express to him forcefully the fatherly affection that His Holiness [?bears] him, the
esteem in which he holds [?His] Majesty's piety and religious zeal, and the pleasure with which he meets the occasions of
giving him signs of it.

R289.summary: Pallotto's audience with Ferdinand II over the Emperor's written answer that blamed the Pope's offices; the date of the Pope's audience for the imperial ambassador.
R289.en:
In accordance with the answer given to my note, of which I sent a copy with the last post, I learned that leading
ministers, and among them Prince Eggenberg, were saying to anyone who gave them occasion that the settlement of these
troubles depended on Our Lord, in whose hands it lay to make the King of France withdraw from Italy, just as he could
also have prevented his coming; but that he had not only not done it of his own accord, but not even when urged by the
instances of the Emperor, who had written him an express letter about it.

R290.summary: Questenberg and the revised imperial answer; Eggenberg on deciding the Mantuan case by justice and the Emperor's coronation in Bologna or Ferrara; Sabran's departure, Wallenstein's gout, Magdeburg, Saxony and the Edict of Restitution.
R290.en:
‹In accordance with this, on the following day› Questenberg came to me. Besides what I had said to His Majesty and to the
Prince, I pointed out to him, regarding His Majesty's remark about the audience given to me, the reflection I made after
returning home: that 27 March, falling on a Tuesday, which is not a day of ordinary audience, made it clear that Our Lord
had given the imperial ambassador an extraordinary audience for this affair, and that he had therefore not delayed even
one day in hearing him. I asked him to tell this to His Majesty, as I am willing to believe he will have done, and I
shall do so myself at the first opportunity.

Today the said Signor Questenberg sent me His Majesty's second answer; from its copy Your Most Illustrious Lordship will
see what has been changed from the first.

R291.summary: The Duke of Neuburg's plans to remarry (a daughter of the Duke of Zweibrücken, a heretic ready to convert) and the Bavarian connection.

R292.summary: Italy and the war preparations; Lorraine and Saarwerden; England and the Palatine; the election of the King of the Romans; Saxony, Brandenburg and Gabor's wife.
R292.en:
Vienna, 18 August 1629. A. 43.

As to the affairs of Italy I have nothing else to report, except that the same ideas and disposition towards peace are
maintained, but no effort is spared to give every greater [443] […] to the provisions for war and to the advance of
troops towards [?the frontiers]. The suspicions of the designs of France and of the [290] keep growing, that they are
aimed at disturbing the affairs of the Empire.

R293.summary: Provisions for the Church in the Empire, Cardinal Klesl's speech, the Dohna affair at Breslau.
R293.en:
‹... he wondered that it had been neglected to conform for the› disposition of the […], and in this too he has promised me
his assistance. I did not think it right to speak of it with His Majesty before hearing the Prince; meanwhile His Majesty
has gone out again to the hunt, where he will stay some weeks. Next week I shall go out to wait on His Majesty and shall
speak to him [609] this business.

As to the provisions of benefices and churches to be recovered, it is true that the Lord Prince declared to me that His
Majesty did not claim, nor would let himself be drawn into claiming, what I was told, as I wrote on 7 April, namely the
ius nominandi pro prima vice, so that he would not even be satisfied if Our Lord provided the persons His Majesty
desired, unless the provisions were made as of persons nominated and presented by His Majesty;

R294.summary: Cardinal Harrach, the Camaldolese foundation stone and the reform of the Augustinians.
R294.en:
‹... he answered that he wishes to please› His Majesty, but that he also wishes to know how he means to treat the
cardinals. What is certain is that the Lord Cardinal, like the others who are subjects, will not depart from the
Emperor's views; and we must pray God that the Emperor does not take a fancy to treat them even worse, for I fear that
they will put up with that too.

I have persuaded the Lord […] that, without declaring that he claims the baldachin, so as not to put himself to this test
and not to irritate His Majesty and his ministers, he should avoid occasions of singing Mass under various pretexts,
which he will not lack; and so far he has excused himself twice, one of them on the occasion of laying the first stone of
the church of the Camaldolese fathers, which he had already promised, and [557] I stood in for His Most Illustrious
Lordship.

R295.summary: How to raise difficulties through the imperial ambassador; Stralendorf and Halberstadt.
R295.en:
When [His Holiness] is inclined, and things are in a state where His Majesty and Signor von Stralendorf can be gratified
with the provostship of Halberstadt, then, so that the favour may be truly recognised as coming from the goodwill of Our
Lord and from the intercession of Your Most Illustrious Lordship, it seems that it would matter a great deal if, when the
Lord Ambassador speaks of it, some difficulty were raised with him: for instance, that the provostship has been asked
for by others and that some expectation of it has been given, as I do not doubt can be said truthfully;

R296.summary: P. Valeriano Magni's control of the Bohemian church-property business and the danger it holds for the nunciature.
R296.en:
What Your Most Illustrious Lordship was pleased to hint to me about the person of Father Magno has been no small relief
to me in bearing his proceedings, of which until now I have written to Your Most Illustrious Lordship only what I judged
I could not keep silent without failing in the precise obligation of your servant and of a good minister of that holy
See; and Your Most Illustrious Lordship may be certain that, as I have borne it until now, so I shall do in future,
however reluctantly, in order to second the wishes of Our Lord and of Your Most Illustrious Lordship.

R297.summary: Wallenstein holding back from Italy; Savoy, the Venetians, the Spanish fleet; honours at court; the restitution of church property.
R297.en:
The latest letters from the Empire of the thirteenth of this month report that the Duke of Mecklenburg [Wallenstein] was
still staying at Halberstadt, without its being known when he would leave, but that he was waiting for news about the
affairs of Italy in order to set out in that direction; but I have word that he is holding back, resolved not to march
into that province with the bulk of the army, and much less in person, unless he has a provision of money, victuals and
munitions of war; and that Collalto had sent a commissary post-haste from Nuremberg to [?Milan] to find out clearly from
that [446] what he is going to give and can actually give for the imperial troops, and to make him understand that,
unless there is a sure and effective assignment, the troops will not march, since he does not want to send them to be
consumed and […] by hunger and hardship.

R298.summary: The brief for Baron Thun's Hungarian priory of the Order of Malta and his demands for privileges.
R298.en:
To Signor Baron von Thun, majordomo of the King of Hungary.

I have given Signor Baron von Thun, majordomo of the King of Hungary, the brief that Your Most Illustrious Lordship
obtained in his favour from Our Lord for the priory of Hungary in case of vacancy; he showed the greatest pleasure at
it, and said he remained most obliged to Our Lord and to Your Most Illustrious Lordship. But at the same time he
declared that his wish was, with the brief of faculty to the Grand Master, [?to be released] immediately, for two
purposes: one, to secure himself against the difficulties that will be raised against him in case of vacancy; the other,
to be able to begin recovering the occupied property of the said priory; and that he would then have liked to be
provided now, ex nunc, with the title of coadjutor, which however he would want directly from the Apostolic See.

R299.en:
[…In]deed, a few days earlier, walking in front of the Emperor in sight of the whole court and of [?many] people gathered
for the ceremony of my laying the first stone of the church of the Camaldolese, I went all the time on the right hand of
the said Duke [of Neuburg]; and although I believe the Duke himself would make no difficulty about giving me precedence,
nevertheless, having seen what happened afterwards in the person of the [?Spanish ambassador] on the day of Our Lady, I
have judged it proper not to put myself in danger of calling into doubt the last state of things, which is in my favour,
and of having to come to some point of ill satisfaction, if a more worthy place were prepared for him, not in a separate
and secret spot but in the same church and chapel; in which case I should have to take it up not with the Duke alone but
with the Emperor too.

R300.summary: Bruneau on Wallenstein's reluctance to go to Italy; a sum of 100,000 scudi; the promotion of Don Cesare.

R301.summary: P. Valeriano's second writing on the Carolina; the Jesuits; breaks off mid-sentence.

R302.summary: Bruneau; Spanish aims; an intercepted letter to Monterrey; Aldringen and Strozzi; Conti and the Duca di Poli.

R303.summary: Wallenstein's haste, the indult for Archduke Leopold Wilhelm, the visitor for Aquileia, Savelli and the promotion.
R303.en:
and if […] he has not had it, on [?Friday] I shall send again, [?this] time with every care.

What I wrote in other letters of the haste with which Wallenstein was being pressed to cross into Italy I heard from
the very mouths of the chief ministers of this court and of the Prince of Eggenberg, indeed from the [?Emperor]
himself; but at the same time I believe I indicated […] difficult, chiefly because it was thought that the Spaniards
could not consider it expedient to their interests.

I shall make use, when the occasion offers, of the information Your Most Illustrious Lordship is pleased to give me
about the indult that it has been resolved to grant to the [690] Leopold William;

R304.summary: P. Valeriano's privileges and patents and Count Slavata; the dignity of the nunciature.

R305.summary: A long discourse with Eggenberg on the Mantuan war; Aldringen at the passes; the Grisons.
R305.en:
In a long conversation I had the day before yesterday with Prince Eggenberg, while we spoke of current Italian affairs,
His Excellency declared that if the King of France wrote to the Emperor to assure him of the good intention His Majesty
had had in coming into Italy, and of not prejudicing the dignity and jurisdiction of His Imperial Majesty, and asked him to
hold the cause and interests of the Duke of Nevers recommended for his sake, and at the same time withdrew his troops from
Montferrat and Susa, Christendom and Italy would at once have peace, and the Most Christian King would see by deeds the
esteem the Emperor has for His Majesty and how much his intercession had been of help and use to the Duke.

R306.summary: Pallotto's offices for peace; the Palatine of Hungary and the Archbishop of Esztergom at court; Lamormain; the Duke of Nevers.
R306.en:
Last week I made effective representations to Prince Eggenberg, and to His Excellency himself, for the settlement of
Italian affairs, as I wrote in other letters of mine, suggesting, as speculative talk and without committing not only the
masters but not even the parties, that the difficulty did not lie in the point of reputation, as they seemed to think,
since on this side it is believed that much advantage would be given to the Emperor's; but in the suspicions and
misgivings that the interested parties conceive, and, as they claim, not without grounds, about the substance: namely
that, once the French have withdrawn, the aim is to have the deposit again;

R307.summary: Hungary and Transylvania; the Carolina still undecided.
R307.en:
‹Of Father Lamormaini I know that on the morning of the Nativity of Our Lady he› spoke most freely and most effectively
with His Majesty on this matter, and when His Majesty unburdened himself on his councillors, he answered plainly that His
Majesty ought not to defer to one man alone, but to such and such, naming four or five others; and though these
particulars are not commonly known, it is known everywhere that the said father opposes this war; but that they have
reassured the Emperor's conscience with the opinion of others, and have impressed on him that he must rather again leave
all the rest at risk than leave his dignity and authority despised in Italy.

R308.summary: The visitor for the diocese of Aquileia; the man sent to negotiate died at Trieste.
R308.en:
They have not been satisfied here with the decision about the matter of the visitor in the diocese of [?Aquileia]; they
have, however, reserved giving me an answer until it has been discussed in council. It has been said in recent days that
the [?Patriarch] had died; it is true that he has been gravely ill, as Your Most Illustrious Lordship will no doubt have
heard. I do not know whether they will want to wait to hear what becomes of him before giving an answer.

I have heard that on the occasion of the said [?illness] they have [?talked] of handing the free election over to the
[?chapter], as the other churches that are principalities of the Empire have it. I do not doubt that His Holiness's
supreme prudence will not be taken unawares.

R309.summary: A hint to a privy councillor that a benefice had been promised to Tilly for a relative.
R309.en:
By the last ordinary post I understand that His Majesty wrote to Our Lord and to Signor [596: Prince Savelli] about the
church of Verden in [...] of Count Adam Schwarzenberg; and from what I know of having hinted at in other letters of mine
on this matter, this request will not have reached Our Lord as news. To one [207: privy councillor] I gave a hint, as of
something that had leaked out here, that it had [?already] been promised to Tilly for a relative of his. [?Werdenberg]
showed much feeling, since His Majesty has much committed himself in this business, and moreover [said] that Tilly's
relative is unfit for this church, being [425: ?a Fleming], and on other counts.

I have managed to obtain copies of the letters written by His Majesty in this matter, which I send enclosed;

R310.summary: Wallenstein's astrology and reluctance to go to Italy; peace and Guastalla; the Duke of Neuburg.
R310.en:
This week I received from Fortiguerra, vicar general of the imperial army and very dear to the General because he writes
his histories, and much more because he holds him to be a great astrologer, the letter of which I send the enclosed copy.
And since pressing the proposal being made for settling the affairs of Italy is not in my hands, and indeed grave
difficulties could be met over the point of the deposit, while on the other hand excluding it seemed to me most
unsuitable, I took it as [404: ?the expedient] to answer him in the form you will see from the copy, which I likewise send
with this. I have other indications that the Duke is utterly averse to going into Italy, chiefly because he believes,
according to astrology, to which he is much addicted, that it would turn out unhappily for him;

R311.summary: Ferdinand II's complaints against the King of France for abasing the imperial dignity in Italy.
R311.en:
On Wednesday I dealt with the Lord Prince of Eggenberg about the affair of Italy, taking occasion of the letter written by
His Majesty to Our Lord, and I said how His Holiness, having made most pressing representations to the Most Christian
King through the nuncio resident there and through Monsieur de Béthune, that Majesty's ambassador to His Holiness, in
accordance with the Emperor's wish, had found various difficulties, which he had communicated to Prince Savelli so that
some way might be found to overcome them; and that for the same purpose new public and general prayers had been ordered
in Rome;

R312.summary: The Spanish ambassadors and Casale; the Empress; Spinola; Flanders and the Dutch.
R312.en:
[as] justified in whole or in part, but leaving the judgement and decision on them entirely free to His Majesty. From the
talk of these Spanish ambassadors I cannot draw any disposition towards peace unless they remain with Casale in one way
or another for security and reputation, and unless Savoy and Guastalla are left content. This supposed, it is no wonder
that Eggenberg, utterly devoted to the Spaniards, holds firm on the usual points, not without the agreement of most of
the councillors, who cannot or dare not go against his opinion. And on the day I was at the hunt, being in the pavilion
with His Majesty, the Empress, talking with me, opened herself with some feeling about this towards the Prince, saying
that they try to make her suspect in this business and to see that she should not even speak of it;

R313.summary: Aquileia and the patriarchate; Eggenberg's remark that without an interim the main business cannot be settled.

snip.cap: Barb.lat. 6960 p. 5: the clear heading Di Vienna 4 di Agosto, a struck-out opening line, then the unbroken figures of the despatch Kiewning printed as Nr. 153

system: Two-digit homophonic substitution with syllable and common-word groups, three-digit nomenclator groups (200-999) for names and titles, and the digits 1 and 8 as nulls/word separators, written as a contiguous digit stream; the same key as Barb.lat. 6956…
